title: Serving Runtime: Architecture, Kernel Scheduling, Profiling & Benchmarking Playbook (Team Wiki)
author: Ava Martinez
summary: Consolidated team wiki for the Redwood serving runtime: architecture overview, kernel scheduler design and heuristics, profiling playbooks, benchmarking suite, release notes, known issues, and operational runbooks.
body:
Purpose

This document is the canonical team wiki for the Redwood serving runtime. It consolidates architecture notes, kernel scheduler design and heuristics, profiling and benchmarking procedures, recent release highlights, known issues with mitigations, and operational runbooks for oncall and SRE engineers. Use this page as the first reference for performance investigations and planned runtime changes.

Audience
- SREs and Runtime Engineers
- Applied ML engineers onboarding models to production
- Performance and reliability engineers

Scope
- Inference serving runtime components (redwood-serving-runtime)
- Kernel selection and scheduling heuristics (kernel-selector)
- Profiling tools and standard playbooks (nsys, torch.profiler, perf, custom trace consumers)
- Benchmarking harness and CI integration (benchmark-runner)
- Runbooks for incidents related to latency, OOMs, and degraded throughput

Overview (short)
Our serving runtime is a GPU-optimized inference engine composed of the following logical components:
- model-loader: loads model shards, quantized weights, and metadata
- batcher: continuous batching queue optimizing latency vs throughput
- kernel-selector: picks execution kernel variants based on model architecture, sequence length, and hardware
- kv-cache-service: prefix caching service with TTL and LRU policies
- runtime-agent: per-node process that coordinates scheduling, memory reservations, and telemetry
- autoscaler: capacity controller for Dedicated and Private deployments

Runtime architecture (detailed)
1) Control plane vs data plane
  - Control plane: model registry, config store, rollout policies (service: redwood-controlplane)
  - Data plane: runtime-agent, batcher, kernel-selector, GPU worker processes (service: redwood-serving-runtime)
2) Data flow
  - API -> ingress -> route policy -> selected model variant -> batcher -> kernel-selector -> GPU worker -> response stream
3) Memory model and KV cache
  - Runtime reserves an ephemeral working set per worker: code cache, KV cache, activation storage. KV cache hit rate is critical for low-cost long-chat workloads.

Kernel scheduling: policies and heuristics
- Goal: minimize tail latency (p95/p99) while maximizing overall tokens_per_second and keeping GPU memory fragmentation low.
- Key signals used by kernel-selector:
  - model_arch (decoder-only, encoder-decoder)
  - sequence_length_distribution (short/medium/long)
  - batch_size and batching window
  - kv_cache_hit_rate and prefix reuse
  - gpu_type (A100, H100, L4), cuda_version, cuDNN/Triton kernels available
- Heuristics (summary):
  1. Short sequences + small batch -> prefer low-latency fused attention kernels.
  2. Long sequences -> prefer segmented attention kernels with KV streaming to reduce memory spikes.
  3. High concurrency -> enable continuous batching with adaptive window (max 10ms or until N tokens).
  4. If GPU memory fragmentation > 30% -> prefer memory-frugal kernels (8-bit quantization path) and trigger defragmentation cycle during low traffic.
- Fallbacks and safety
  - If selected kernel fails at runtime (OOM or kernel launch error), kernel-selector automatically falls back to the compatible CPU-bound path or next-safe kernel variant and emits alert KERNEL_FALLBACK.

Profiling playbook (step-by-step)
Purpose: gather repeatable traces to diagnose latency spikes, kernel stalls, and memory growth.
Prerequisites: access to cluster namespace, kube access (k8s), node ssh for nvtop/nsys when necessary, and a representative prompt set.

1) Baseline metrics (quick)
  - Check dashboards: tokens_per_second, p50/p95/p99 latency, gpu_utilization, kv_cache_hit_rate.
  - Note the timeframe, service revision, and request trace ids.
2) Reproduce under controlled load
  - Use benchmark-runner with the representative prompt set and matching concurrency: ./tools/benchmark-runner --model my-model:rev --concurrency 16 --duration 300 --prometheus-endpoint <url>
3) Capture system-level traces (short)
  - nsys: nsys profile --output=trace.nsys --trace=cuda,nvtx --sample=cpu --capture-range=nvtx -- <command to run worker>
  - nvprof (fallback): nvprof --profile-from-start off --target-processes all --export-profile nvprof_out.json <command>
4) Capture PyTorch / Triton traces
  - torch.profiler: use the standard trace wrapper in runtime-agent for 10 warmup iterations then 50 measured iterations.
  - Ensure profiler writes to the central trace-bucket: s3://redwood-traces/runtime/<date>/model_rev/<trace>.json
5) Analyze traces
  - Look for GPU kernel durations, launch latency, CUDA sync events, memory alloc/free patterns.
  - Key indicators: long kernel launch latency (>2ms), frequent small allocations (<1ms) causing fragmentation, or repeated kernel fallback events.
6) Record findings and actions
  - Open a tracking ticket with labels runtime/perf and include trace ids, node ids, and suggested mitigation.

Common profiling commands (examples)
- kubectl logs -n runtime svc/redwood-serving-runtime --since=2h | grep "KERNEL_FALLBACK"
- ./tools/benchmark-runner --model my-model:1.8 --concurrency 8 --prompt-file tests/prompt-sets/chat-small.json --duration 120
- nsys profile -o /tmp/trace --trace=cuda,nvtx --sample=cpu --capture-range=nvtx -- ./bin/runtime-worker --model-config /etc/models/my-model.json
- python -m torch.profiler --schedule wait=1,warmup=2,active=5 --trace-handles cpu,cuda --output /tmp/torch-trace

Benchmarking suite: components and CI
- Components:
  - benchmark-runner: CLI harness that drives workloads, collects traces, and writes metrics to Prometheus and S3.
  - workload-definitions: YAML profiles for chat-short, chat-long, embedding-batch, and rerank workloads.
  - perf-dashboard: Grafana dashboards for historical comparisons.
- Metrics collected:
  - tokens_per_second, requests_per_second, p50/p95/p99 latency (ms), gpu_utilization(%), memory_used(MiB), kv_cache_hit_rate(%), cost_per_token($).
- Example workload YAML (use as template):
  workload_name: chat-long
  concurrency: 8
  prompt_set: tests/prompt-sets/chat-long.json
  target_duration_sec: 600
  model_variant: my-model:quant8
- CI integration:
  - Benchmarks run on main branch for performance regressions; nightly runs on a dedicated perf cluster.
  - Pull requests that touch runtime or kernels must add a benchmark-run job and not decrease tokens_per_second by >5% on the representative small_chat workload.

SLOs and thresholds (operational table)
| Metric | Target | Alert condition | Owner |
|---|---:|---|---|
| p95 latency (1k tokens) | < 350 ms | p95 > 500 ms for 10m | runtime-sre |
| p99 latency | < 650 ms | p99 > 1s for 5m | runtime-sre |
| tokens_per_second (cluster) | > 750k TPS | sustained drop > 15% for 15m | platform-eng |
| GPU utilization (cluster avg) | 65-90% | < 40% or > 95% | infra-eng |
| kv_cache_hit_rate | > 70% | < 50% | serving-runtime-eng |

Release notes (recent highlights)
- 2026-11-15: v2.6.1
  - Kernel-selector: new adaptive-window heuristic for continuous batching reduced p95 by 18% on small_chat.
  - Memory management: background defragmentation reduced transient OOMs by 40%.
  - Observability: added KERNEL_SELECT_LATENCY metric and trace correlation ids.
- 2026-08-02: v2.5.0
  - Introduced quant8 execution path with optional accuracy guardrails.
  - Benchmark harness: added embedding-batch workload and cost_per_token estimation.

Known issues and workarounds
1) Long-sequence OOMs on H100 with very large context (>64k tokens)
  - Symptom: worker terminates with OOM during large-generation tests.
  - Mitigation: enable segmented_attention and set runtime.conf.max_sequence_length=65536; if unsuccessful, use model sharding or move to Dedicated pool with larger Vram.
2) High p99 when kv_cache_hit_rate drops suddenly
  - Symptom: p99 spikes while throughput remains stable.
  - Mitigation: confirm cache TTL aligned with client behavior; increase cacheSize for hot models and enable prefix_coalescing to improve hit rate.
3) Kernel fallback due to cuda driver mismatch after node upgrade
  - Symptom: KERNEL_FALLBACK logs and elevated kernel_fallback_count.
  - Mitigation: pin cuda/driver versions via node image; redeploy runtime-worker with compatible cuDNN and log the driver mismatch for platform team.

Runtime runbooks (incident playbooks)
1) Latency increase (p95/p99)
  - Step 1: Triage dashboards, note model variant and recent rollouts.
  - Step 2: Check KERNEL_FALLBACK events: kubectl -n runtime logs svc/redwood-serving-runtime | grep "KERNEL_FALLBACK"
  - Step 3: Run quick-profile on a single worker using benchmark-runner with --concurrency 4 and collect nsys trace.
  - Step 4: If kernel-launch latency > 2ms, roll back to previous kernel configuration or disable new kernel via feature flag: runtime.feature.disable_kernel_x=true
  - Step 5: If fallback occurs for multiple nodes, scale down traffic via routing policy to reduce pressure and open pager.
2) Memory growth / OOMs
  - Step 1: Identify node and worker: kubectl describe pod <pod> and check dmesg for OOM events.
  - Step 2: Temporarily reduce max_concurrency on the node: kubectl patch node <node> --patch '{"metadata":{"annotations":{"runtime/max_concurrency":"4"}}}'
  - Step 3: Trigger background defragmentation on runtime-agent: ./bin/runtime-agent --defrag && monitor memory metrics.
  - Step 4: If persistent, move model to Dedicated pool with guaranteed allocation.

Ownership and escalation
- Primary owners: serving-runtime-eng (team slack: #serving-runtime, oncall rotation: serving-runtime-sre)
- Pager escalation: runtime-sre -> infra-eng -> platform-eng -> CTO on critical incidents

Team wiki links and references
- Model onboarding: /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/model-onboarding
- Benchmark harness repo: github.com/redwood-inference/benchmark-runner
- Trace storage: s3://redwood-traces/runtime/
- Observability dashboards: Grafana link (internal)

How to contribute
- Add or update workload YAML under infra/perf/workloads.
- If you add kernels or change kernel selection heuristics, add a benchmark PR with performance numbers and a brief analysis.
- For security-sensitive changes (e.g., telemetry), tag reviewers from security-and-compliance.

Appendix: Quick config snippet (runtime.conf)
[runtime]
batching_window_ms = 8
max_batch_size = 32
enable_adaptive_window = true
segmented_attention = false
kv_cache_ttl_seconds = 86400
max_sequence_length = 32768
quantization_profile = "quant8"

Notes
- Keep this page updated with new kernel variants and benchmark baselines.
- For long investigations, attach trace ids and a short executive summary to the ticket.
